claim: The Palestinians are recent immigrants; there is no Palestinian people.

heard.who: Newt Gingrich, then a US presidential candidate, to The Jewish Channel, December 2011 (as reported by The New York Times)
heard.quote: I think that we've had an invented Palestinian people, who are in fact Arabs, and were historically part of the Arab community.

heard.who: Golda Meir, Israeli prime minister, to The Sunday Times, 1969 (as quoted by historian Zachary Foster in Foreign Affairs)
heard.quote: When was there an independent Palestinian people with a Palestinian state?

heard.who: Daniel Pipes, writing in 1986 in support of Joan Peters's book From Time Immemorial
heard.quote: Miss Peters's central thesis is that a substantial immigration of Arabs to Palestine took place during the first half of the twentieth century.

answer: Part of this is false and part is a real argument. Arabs conquered the land in the 630s; Arabic and Islam spread gradually over centuries, mostly by conversion, not replacement. Muslims and Christians were the large majority in every count: about 94 percent in 1917, 78 percent Muslim in the 1922 census, 73 percent in 1931. The idea that most arrived in the Mandate years, argued by Joan Peters in 1984, was rejected by most reviewers; British and UN analysts found Arab growth came almost entirely from births. The highest serious estimate (Gottheil) puts immigration at about a third of growth in Jewish-settled districts in 1922-31, partly internal movement. A distinct Palestinian national identity is dated by historians from 1909 to the early 1920s or, by one, after 1948. Being a modern identity does not make a people recent arrivals.

facts.text: Arab armies conquered the land in the 630s; Arabic and Islam spread gradually, over centuries, and most of the population converted over time rather than being replaced.

facts.text: Historians date the emergence of a distinct Palestinian national identity differently: the first known Arab use of the word 'Palestinian' is from 1909 and it was used in newspapers in 1910-1913 (Zachary Foster); Rashid Khalidi dates the formation of that identity to 1917-1923, after the First World War; Issam Nassar says it crystallised after contact with Zionism and spread through the Mandate; Efraim Karsh holds that the separation and dispersal after 1948 prevented a cohesive national identity from crystallising.

facts.text: Joan Peters's 1984 book From Time Immemorial argued that a substantial Arab immigration took place in the first half of the 20th century. Reviewers found her use of statistics and sources unreliable: even Daniel Pipes, who accepted her thesis, said the book 'quotes carelessly, uses statistics sloppily, and ignores inconvenient facts', and Yehoshua Porath and Ian Gilmour showed that her key figures and her reading of the Hope Simpson report were wrong.

facts.text: Demographers' estimates of Arab immigration range from minimal to substantial in one region: Justin McCarthy concluded that Muslim immigration after 1870 was small (Gottheil reports that McCarthy used Roberto Bachi's figure of about 900 Arab immigrants a year caught entering illegally in 1931-45); Gottheil estimates that Arab movement into the sub-districts that became Israel was as much as 38.7 percent of the 1922-31 Arab growth there, but also says the total is unknown and the figure includes Arabs moving within Palestine; Bachi himself wrote, as Gottheil quotes him, that total immigration could not even be guessed.

sources.quote: The 1922-1931 Arab immigration alone represents 11.8 percent of the total Arab settled population of 1931 and as much as 38.7 percent of the total 1922-1931 Arab population growth.

contested: Estimates of Arab immigration are disputed. McCarthy (1990, 'the single most cited' study of the subject, per Gottheil) finds immigration minimal; Gottheil argues McCarthy used Bachi's figure of 900 illegal immigrants a year, which Bachi said counted only those caught, and that the official data cannot show unrecorded entry. Gottheil's 38.7 percent (1971) and 36.8 percent (2003) are for sub-districts that became Israel, and he says part of the gain was Arabs moving there from elsewhere in Palestine, which Porath and Bachi also describe. The card reports both ends; it does not say the true figure is known.

Pipes wrote that Peters's central thesis had not been refuted and that her critics should go back to the archives; Porath and Gilmour answered with specific errors. Peters's book was widely praised on publication and widely rejected within two years. The card cites Porath and Gilmour as critics.

Whether a 'Palestinian people' existed before the 20th century is a question about when a national identity formed, which historians date differently (Foster: first used 1909; Khalidi: 1917-23, with older local loyalties; Karsh: not cohesive after 1948). Khalidi writes that Palestinian and other Arab national identities are modern, as are most national identities. Other scholars (Gerber, Kimmerling) date elements earlier, per Tezcan's survey of the literature, which the checker could not read.
Foster says Golda Meir's 1969 words were 'there were no such thing as Palestinians'; the card quotes only the part Foster quotes verbatim.
could_not_verify: A readable source for the Muslim majority from the end of the 12th century on (Bachi, DellaPergola): the tables are in a PDF the checker cannot read, so the fact starts in the 19th century.
Joan Peters's own words: only Pipes's summary of her thesis was read; her book is not online in a readable form.

The 1946 UNSCOP figures and the claim that most growth was natural increase rest on one UN source plus government and single-author pieces; only the Gottheil/Porath numbers have three independent sites.

A statement of the share of Arab growth due to immigration from a demographer who is neither Gottheil nor McCarthy: not found on a readable page. The Journal of Palestine Studies article that puts natural increase at 96 percent of Muslim growth in 1922-45 is a PDF and was not read. McCarthy's own text is a PDF; his view is cited through Gottheil, who disputes it.

The 1931 census on three independent readable sites: only ECF and CIE (advocacy) were read; the PASSIA summary returned an error. Gerber and Kimmerling on earlier dating (via Tezcan, a PDF): not cited as a source.
not_claimed: That Palestinian national identity is ancient, or that it is recent: historians disagree on the date, and the card reports the positions.
That no Arab immigration into Mandate Palestine happened: some did, and the size is uncertain.
That the length of time a people has had a national identity decides its rights or the outcome of any modern political question.
That Jews do not have a historical tie to the land: see the Jewish presence card.
